## Today

We discuss @smith_brays:2026, a nonstationary flood frequency analysis of Brays Bayou at Houston, fit by Bayesian methods in the open-source RMC-BestFit software from the US Army Corps of Engineers.

::: {.callout-important}
Every figure is from the paper, which is open access under CC BY 4.0, so it's OK to share here.
:::

## Case study: two Texas watersheds

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![Brays Bayou and O.C. Fisher Reservoir [@smith_brays:2026, Fig. 1, CC BY 4.0].](smith-fig1-map.png){height=6cm}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
Clear physical drivers and strong nonstationary signals

- **Brays Bayou:** floods rising with urbanization
- **O.C. Fisher:** floods falling with brush encroachment and groundwater pumping

# The data

## The record is a modeling choice

![Annual maximum instantaneous flow at USGS 08075000, 1929-2024; the shaded band is 1930-1935, when only a perception threshold is known [@smith_brays:2026, Fig. 2, CC BY 4.0].](smith-fig2-chronology.png){height=75%}

## The likelihood

The stationary likelihood [@smith_brays:2026, eq. 1]:

$$
L(\mathbf{x} \mid \theta) = \prod_{i=1}^{N} f(x_i \mid \theta)
$$

::: {.fragment}
In the **nonstationary model** the parameters depend on the year, $\theta_t$ [@smith_brays:2026, eq. 2]:

$$
L(\mathbf{x} \mid \theta) = \prod_{t=1}^{T} f(x_t \mid \theta_t)
$$
:::

## A perception threshold is a censored observation

A perception threshold is "the flow above which an event would have been recorded in any given year" [@smith_brays:2026, p. 11, eq. 3].

$$
L(\mathbf{x} \mid \theta) = \prod_{t=1}^{T}
\begin{cases}
f(x_t \mid \theta_t) & \text{exact data} \\
F(x_t^{U} \mid \theta_t) & \text{left censored (below threshold)} \\
1 - F(x_t^{L} \mid \theta_t) & \text{right censored (above threshold)} \\
F(x_t^{U} \mid \theta_t) - F(x_t^{L} \mid \theta_t) & \text{interval censored}
\end{cases}
$$

$f$ is the probability density and $F$ the cumulative distribution function.

## Brays Bayou likelihood

- 1929 and 1936-2024: $f(x_t \mid \theta_t)$.
- Each of 1930-1935: $F(994 \mid \theta_t)$.

A year with no measured flood still carries information: six years in a row below 994 m³/s rules out parameter values that make 994 m³/s common.

For more, read @gelman_bda3:2014, §8.7, on censored data in a Bayesian model.

| Unequal-variance $t$-test | $\mu_1 = \mu_2$ | $5.91 \times 10^{-12}$ |

## The autocorrelation of a trending record

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![Autocorrelation of the Brays annual maxima out to lag 20, with 95% bounds [@smith_brays:2026, Fig. 3, CC BY 4.0].](smith-fig3-acf.png){height=6cm}
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}

- Nearly every lag out to 20 sits above the bound.
- A trend does this: early years are all low and late years all high, so any two years close in time look alike.
- The paper reads it as "characteristic of a strong monotonic trend" [@smith_brays:2026, p. 13].
:::
:::

# The model

## Log-Pearson Type III

LP3 is used "consistent with federal guidelines established in Bulletin 17C" [@smith_brays:2026, p. 8].

- Like the GEV, it is fit to annual maxima.
- "Log" means it is fit to $\log_{10}$ of the flow.
- Think: log-normal with a skewness parameter added.
  - Positive means prone to floods far above the mean
  - Negative means the watershed caps the largest flow.
  - The skew is often similar at nearby gauges -- we will revisit this next week!

## Trend formulas the software offers

| Model | Formulation | Use case in the paper |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Constant | $\mu_t = \alpha$ | No detectable trend |
| Linear | $\mu_t = \alpha + \beta t$ | Gradual urban expansion |
| Exponential | $\mu_t = \alpha e^{-\beta t}$ | Trend slowing as a watershed stabilizes |
| Logistic | $\mu_t = \frac{\alpha}{1 + e^{-\beta t}}$ | Sprawl that plateaus |
| Power | $\mu_t = \alpha t^{\beta}$ | Accelerating imperviousness |
| Quadratic | $\mu_t = \alpha + \beta t + \gamma t^{2}$ | Rise then plateau |
| Cubic | $\mu_t = \alpha + \beta t + \gamma t^{2} + \delta t^{3}$ | Sequential land-use changes |
| Sinusoidal | $\mu_t = \alpha + \beta \sin(2 \pi \gamma t + \delta)$ | Multidecadal climate cycles |
| Step | $\mu_t = \mu_1$ for $t \le t_c$, $\mu_2$ for $t > t_c$ | A land-cover change in a known year |

## Time is the covariate

::: {.callout-tip}
## Think

Monday's recipe said to choose a covariate by mechanism.
What does $t$ _stand in_ for at Brays?
:::

::: {.fragment}

- Imperviousness and channelization, neither of which is in the model.
- The authors say so: "formal covariate-based attribution is beyond the current scope" [@smith_brays:2026, p. 13].
:::

## Bayes' theorem in Smith's notation

@smith_brays:2026, eq. 4:

$$
p(\theta \mid \mathbf{x}) = \frac{L(\mathbf{x} \mid \theta) \cdot \pi(\theta)}{\int L(\mathbf{x} \mid \theta) \cdot \pi(\theta) d\theta}
$$

The joint prior over $p$ parameters, then with the parameters independent [@smith_brays:2026, eqs. 5-6]:

$$
\pi(\theta) = \pi(\theta_1 \cap \theta_2 \cap \cdots \cap \theta_p)
$$

$$
\pi(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^{p} f(\theta_i)
$$

## The default priors

- Flat priors on location, scale, and shape, "centered near the likelihood with broad spread" [@smith_brays:2026, p. 5].
- A Jeffreys prior on the scale, $\pi(\sigma) \propto 1/\sigma$, "equivalent to using a log-link function" (p. 5).
- That is a flat prior on $\log \sigma$: the same log scale Monday's model used for $\sigma$.
- Trend parameters (slopes, change points) get uninformative priors, and priors on the other parameters apply at the final year $T$ (p. 6).

## Prior information on a flood quantile

A quantile prior puts a distribution on the flood $x_p$ with annual exceedance probability $p$, with hyperparameters $\theta_h$ [@smith_brays:2026, eq. 7]:

$$
h(x_p) = f(x_p \mid \theta_h)
$$

The quantile is a function of the parameters in the final year [@smith_brays:2026, eq. 8]:

$$
x_p = F^{-1}(p \mid \theta_T)
$$

## A quantile prior becomes a prior on the parameters

Substitute to evaluate it in parameter space [@smith_brays:2026, eq. 9]:

$$
\pi_q(\theta) = h\left(F^{-1}(p \mid \theta_T)\right)
$$

The posterior multiplies in every source [@smith_brays:2026, eq. 10]:

$$
p(\theta \mid \mathbf{x}) \propto L(\mathbf{x} \mid \theta) \cdot \pi(\theta) \cdot \pi_q(\theta)
$$

"The quantile prior acts as a penalty function, rewarding parameter sets that produce flood quantiles consistent with the prior information" (p. 6).
O.C. Fisher uses one, taken from a rainfall-runoff model; Brays does not.

## Sampling the posterior

RMC-BestFit samples with DE-MCzs, a differential-evolution Markov chain with a "snooker update" [@smith_brays:2026, p. 9].

- It uses no gradients.
- It scales poorly to many parameters, where the NUTS sampler you used in `Turing` scales well (by leveraging gradients)
- It can do better on a posterior with several modes, or a likelihood with discrete parameters, such as the step model's change year $t_c$.

## The posterior predictive distribution

The full distribution of a flood $k$ years into the future [@smith_brays:2026, eq. 14]:

$$
p(x_{T+k} \mid \mathbf{x}) = \int f(x_{T+k} \mid \theta_{T+k}) \cdot p(\theta \mid \mathbf{x}) d\theta
$$

- It "accounts for both parameter uncertainty (epistemic) and natural variability (aleatory)" (p. 10), as in labs 4 and 5.
  - This is a _narrow_ definition of epistemic uncertainty
- Think of it as "averaging over the posterior"

## Four plausible models

![The 2-year return level under (a) the stationary, (b) linear-logistic, (c) logistic-logistic, and (d) step-logistic models, with 90% credible intervals [@smith_brays:2026, Fig. 4, CC BY 4.0].](smith-fig4-trends.png){height=90%}

## The fitted change point and the variance

- The change point is estimated at 1968, near the start of Houston's most intensive development in the early 1970s [@smith_brays:2026, p. 14].
- The location jumps at the change point, while the scale, the spread of the log-flows, declines smoothly over the whole record with no jump (logistic, $\beta = -0.014$).
- Early floods spanned about 20-300 m³/s, more than a factor of ten; after urbanization, about 200-800 m³/s, a factor of four (p. 14).

## Why urbanization narrows the log-space spread

"In a pre-urbanization watershed, flood magnitudes are highly variable because antecedent soil moisture, infiltration capacity, and vegetation interception modulate rainfall-runoff partitioning differently for each event" [@smith_brays:2026, p. 23].

Pave it over and the response "approaches a near-deterministic conversion of rainfall to runoff" (p. 24).

# Discussion

## Step Model

::: {.callout-tip}
## Think

The selected model has one level before 1968 and one after, forever.
What would violate that?
:::

::: {.pause}

- More urbanization after 1968.
- More infrastructure: channelization and detention basins.
:::

## How you might address it

- A better covariate: impervious area fraction in place of the year, which the paper names as future work [@smith_brays:2026, p. 25].
- A different method: fit the extreme value model to rainfall, and run it through a flood model that represents land use and infrastructure.
- The paper's own list adds hierarchical pooling across sites, model averaging over the trend forms, and alternative distributions (pp. 24-25).
